BOSTON — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
Angel Martínez had three hits for the Guardians, who entered the day with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the division. Chicago owns the tiebreaker by winning the season series. Cleveland stranded 15 baserunners.
The loss was Boston’s eighth in 12 games, spoiling Chad Tracy’s first game as manager after the club named him its 49th in team history.
Adley Rutschman added three hits for Boston, which clinched one of the AL’s wild-card spots on Sunday.
Boston pinch hitter Mickey Gasper hit Hunter Gaddis’ first pitch, tying it at 2-2 leading off the eighth.
Gaddis (5-3) got the win and Cade Smith recorded the final three outs for his 40th save.
Miller (4-2) hit a batter and gave up two hits in an inning.
A strong candidate for the AL Rookie of the Year, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick gave up a run over five innings. He lowered his ERA to 2.55 and is on pace to become the fourth rookie starting pitcher in MLB history with an ERA under 2.60 and averaging 9.0 or more strikeouts per nine innings.
In his tune-up for a likely playoff start next week, Boston lefty Payton Tolle struggled with his control over 5 2/3 innings, giving up two runs on eight hits.
Up next
Guardians LHP Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67 ERA) is set to face Red Sox RHP Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.82) on Wednesday in the middle game of the three-game series.

item.content:encoded:
In this purgatorial period for the Red Sox, after they clinched a playoff berth over the weekend and before they open the postseason next week, what matters?
The result Tuesday, a 3-2 loss to the Guardians at Fenway Park, was not of major significance.
Of greater note was the how — and what those trends may portend heading into the most important time of year: another ugly outing for reliever Erik Miller, and another night of minimal hitting for the lineup.
The Red Sox (84-73) have dropped three games in a row and eight of their past 12.
“We’ve still got five games to play, and you [have to] keep guys out there and engaged and ready to roll,” manager Chad Tracy said. “I told the guys before, we earned the right to be in position to be able to line things up. That being said, we still want to go out and win the games. We had a chance to tonight.”
Miller inherited a tied game in the ninth inning and struggled again, allowing a game-deciding run and throwing 22 pitches (10 strikes). He hit his first batter, Chase DeLauter, with a pitch. DeLauter eventually scored on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly. Altogether, Miller yielded two hits and a walk.
In September, the Sox’ theoretical top lefthanded setup man has one clean inning in seven attempts, a 8.53 ERA, and a 2.37 WHIP.
Miller said his patience with himself — and a mechanical issue he is trying to fix — is “definitely running thin at this point.”
“I’d be lying if I say otherwise,” he said. “I would like to have been through this by now, be over it. But … there’s no way I can feel better and work through it without throwing [in] a game. So that’s just how it’s going to have to be: keep throwing, get through it.”
Tracy, noting that Miller will pitch in a couple more games before the regular season ends Sunday, added: “I thought today was even another step in the right direction.”
Offensively, the Red Sox had few highlights. Mickey Gasper launched a pinch-hit tying home run off setup man Hunter Gaddis to lead off the eighth, but the Sox totaled nine runners stranded on base and went 0 for 9 with men in scoring position.
In the positives column: Adley Rutschman finished 3 for 4, with two doubles (and a line out to deep center) coming against lefthanders.
Entering the game, Rutschman was 2 for 26 with no extra-base hits against lefties as a member of the Red Sox.
“Being a switch hitter has a lot that goes into it, and you go through phases where you’re hitting good [from] one side and not the other and it flip flops sometimes and then goes back,” Rutschman said. “I want to be in a good spot, especially with the playoffs coming up.”
In a matchup between perhaps the top two rookie pitchers this year, Payton Tolle (5⅔ innings, two runs) was almost equal to fellow lefthander Parker Messick (five innings, one run) of the Guardians.
Tolle slogged through a 22-pitch second frame, during which he allowed three hits and two walks but managed to hold the AL Central-leading Guardians (82-75) to the two runs.
When Tracy pulled him in the sixth, Tolle walked off the Fenway mound — for potentially the last time this year — to a standing ovation from the fans behind the home dugout. He waved back to them.
“I think he’s won them over pretty significantly,” Tracy said.
Tolle finished his rookie season with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148⅔ innings (26 starts).
Up next: a start in the AL Wild Card Series.
“It’s the postseason. This is what we play for,” Tolle said. “But it is what it is. We go on, and we have a job to do.”

For all intents and purposes, none of these last games down the stretch mean anything to the Red Sox. They have already punched their ticket to the playoffs and nothing that happens from here on out will change that.
But while readying themselves for the games that matter, the Red Sox would still prefer to go into the postseason with some momentum, and Tuesday’s performance was at times pretty hard to watch.
Playing without three projected postseason starters, the Red Sox suffered a listless 3-2 loss in their series opener against the Cleveland Guardians. Despite a game-tying pinch hit home run by Mickey Gasper in the bottom of the eighth, the Red Sox gave the lead right back in the ninth, capping off a night riddled with poor decisions and uncharacteristic mistakes.
Reliever Erik Miller saw his struggles continue by allowing two hits, a walk, a hit batsman and the go-ahead sacrifice fly by Angel Martinez in the top of the ninth, and outside of Gasper and Adley Rutschman going 3 for 4 with two doubles and a run scored, there wasn’t much to write home about as the Red Sox suffered their third straight defeat.
Making his final start before the playoffs, Payton Tolle wasn’t as sharp as he would’ve hoped, but once again he gave the Red Sox a chance to win.
After posting a scoreless first, Tolle allowed two runs and five baserunners over the course of a challenging second inning. He started by giving up a leadoff double, had a soft grounder from David Fry deflect off his leg and into the outfield for an RBI single, and allowed another single and a walk to load the bases with nobody out.
Tolle was able to minimize the damage from there, allowing a second run to score on a double play ball by Brayan Rocchio before escaping the inning. He continued facing traffic for the rest of his outing but grinded his way into the sixth and departed to a standing ovation from the Fenway Park faithful.
Tolle finished with two runs allowed on eight hits, two walks and a hit batsman over 5 2/3 innings with five strikeouts. He fell one out short of recording another quality start, leaving him with 13 in 26 outings, and he ends his rookie year with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.
The Red Sox got a run back in the bottom of the second after Adley Rutschman led off with a double and came around to score on an RBI groundout by Andruw Monasterio, but otherwise the bats struggled against Guardians rookie Parker Messick. The left-hander, who came into the game with a 2.57 ERA and projects as a possible AL Cy Young Award finalist, limited the Red Sox to one run on five hits over five innings.
One thing Boston was able to do was drive up the rookie’s pitch count, particularly in the fourth when Monasterio was able to work a 12-pitch walk. That helped force the lefty from the game after five, giving the Red Sox a chance to try their luck against Cleveland’s bullpen.
The Red Sox let a golden opportunity go to waste in the bottom of the sixth, leaving men at second and third, but Alec Gamboa kept it a one-run game in the top of the seventh despite the Guardians taking advantage of some sloppy baseball to get runners at second and third themselves with one out.
Cleveland’s Fry, who had already grounded into a fielder’s choice where the runner was thrown out at the plate earlier in the third inning, did so a second time for the second out of the seventh, and Gamboa struck out former No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana to end the inning.
Then, in the bottom of the eighth, Gasper struck for his 10th home run of the season, hitting the first pitch he saw from Guardians reliever Hunter Gaddis 390 feet to the right field stands.
The good vibes didn’t last long.
Miller, who had proven an impactful bullpen addition since his arrival at the trade deadline, saw his recent control issues continue with his latest ugly outing. The left-hander hit the first batter he faced, gave up the lead on a sacrifice fly by Martinez and eventually loaded the bases before getting a fly out to keep things from spiraling further.
Miller has now allowed six runs and six walks over his past 3 1/3 innings, a trend the Red Sox can’t afford to continue if he’s to remain a high-leverage option in the playoffs.

The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

SAN FRANCISCO — First, the good news: outfielder Bo Davidson and infielder Marcelo Mayer will make their long-awaited Giants debuts on Monday night at Oracle Park against the Minnesota Twins. Now, the bad: Bryce Eldridge and Jung Hoo Lee became the latest players to hit the injured list.
Mayer, acquired at the trade deadline from the Boston Red Sox, was reinstated from the injured list, while Davidson was called up from Triple-A Sacramento. Davidson will play right field and bat third in his major-league debut, while Mayer will bat fourth and be the team’s designated hitter.
“Just showing them what I can do and giving them the best I can every game until the season’s over,” Davidson said when asked what he could provide. “Just showing them what Bo is.”
What is Bo?
“You’ll see,” Davidson said with a smile.
Meanwhile, Eldridge landed on the seven-day concussion list after bumping his head at the team’s hotel in Los Angeles, while Lee landed on the 10-day injured list with a groin contusion after fouling a ball off himself on Sunday. Lee’s season is over, and manager Tony Vitello said he doesn’t anticipate Eldridge will play again this season, which ends Sunday.
With Lee landing on the injured list, every member of the Opening Day lineup is either on the injured list (Lee, Willy Adames, Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman, Logan Webb, Casey Schmitt, Harrison Bader) or has been traded (Patrick Bailey, Heliot Ramos, Luis Arraez). The only players from the Opening Day roster still on the roster are infielder Christian Koss and right-hander Landen Roupp.
Adames (left elbow sprain) took grounders and batting practice on Monday afternoon, but he’s very unlikely to return before the end of the season.
Eldridge, who will turn 22 next month, exceeded expectations as a rookie and should be a foundational piece of the Giants’ lineup alongside Devers. Over 107 games, Eldridge hit .269/.364/.461 with 17 home runs, 23 doubles and 57 RBIs. Among rookies, Eldridge’s 130 wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) was the third-highest in the majors.
“Incredibly impressive,” Vitello said of Eldridge’s season. “We summarized that a little bit with him this morning in there. Maturity is the word that gets thrown around a bunch, but it got thrown around in there, too. I think consistency is the other word. He attached that to himself in a good way, not in a braggadocious way.
“If I could speak for him through his own words, a big difference between last year and this year is understanding the ups and downs and how to maintain consistency, which is a lot easier to formulate or plan out than it is to put into act.”
Along with the offense, Vitello also highlighted Eldridge’s defense, which was his biggest question as a prospect. After committing 18 errors in 2024 and 9 in 2025, Eldridge only had two errors this season in the majors and minors. Eldridge also graded out well by Baseball Savant’s new first baseman receiving metric.
Going into next season, one area where Vitello believes Eldridge can improve is baserunning.
“He’s got good instincts, but there’s so many things that he’s seeing for the first time in his life, literally,” Vitello said. “Safety bunts, stuff like that. And then on the base running … he didn’t do anything that would cause us to jump here in the dugout or cost us big, but for a guy that’s going to be on base as often as he is — and he’s not a burner — he’s got to be good on those little separators of reads, preparation before a pitch.”
Davidson, 24, is the Giants’ No. 5 prospect, per Baseball America. Over 125 games this season with Double-A Richmond and Triple-A Sacramento, Davidson hit .290 with 29 home runs, 20 steals and 94 RBIs. He was a candidate to get called up earlier this month but missed a week after fouling a ball off his foot on Sept. 9.
For all of Davidson’s production on the field, he believes the biggest area he’s grown has been “being a better man off the field.”
Davidson is one of many intriguing prospects in a farm system that has climbed the rankings. Along with Davidson, the Giants’ farm system is headlined by shortstops Josuar Gonzalez and Luis Hernandez, as well as right-handed pitcher Jackson Flora.
“We’ve got a very special group of guys that’s coming through,” said Davidson, whose mother, brother, girlfriend and daughter will be in attendance. “The farm itself, the numbers this year just showed. Us being really good brothers off the field, it just shows on the field with the chemistry.”
“I’m excited to see Bo again,” Vitello said. “Just kind of knowing who he was in high school and junior college. … We were able to get him some action in spring training, and then you’re following along, following along. We knew [his promotion] would happen at some point.”
Mayer, 23, was traded to the Giants on Aug. 3 from the Boston Red Sox in exchange for lefty reliever Erik Miller and minor-league outfielder Carlos Gutierrez. The infielder had been recovering from a bone stress reaction to the left ulna, as well as a bone bruise on his right foot.
Vitello anticipates Mayer will primarily be the team’s designated hitter over the final six games, but he could also see some time in the infield.

The San Francisco Giants are down to two members of their Opening Day roster still active with the club after placing first baseman Bryce Eldridge and right fielder Jung Hoo Lee on the injured list Monday.
Eldridge landed on the seven-day concussion injured list after getting hurt in the team's Los Angeles hotel on Friday, according to the team. He didn't play in the series as the Dodgers swept three games.
His IL move is retroactive to Friday, leaving open the possibility he could return to action before the season ends this weekend, but manager Tony Vitello told reporters that Eldridge likely will be shut down for the rest of the campaign.
Lee was placed on the 10-day IL due to a groin contusion, so his season is over. He exited San Francisco's 3-1 loss to the Dodgers on Sunday in the seventh inning, an inning after fouling a pitch off his groin.
Right-hander Landen Roupp and shortstop Christian Koss are the last players on the Giants' active roster who were with the team when the season started, though neither was in the lineup on March 25 against the New York Yankees. Many of the other players from the season-opening roster were either part of the team's sell-off at the trade deadline or are on the IL.
Eldridge, 21, has a .269 batting average, a .364 on-base percentage and a .461 slugging percentage with 17 homers and 57 RBIs in 107 games this year. He began his major league career with San Francisco in 2025, hitting .107 with no homers in 10 games.
Lee, 28, batting .276/.320/.404 with 10 home runs and 57 RBIs in 143 games this season. Through three years with the Giants, he has a .270/.322/.397 batting line with 20 homers and 120 RBIs over 330 games.
The Giants filled the two roster vacancies by activating infielder Marcelo Mayer from the injured list and promoting outfielder Bo Davidson from Triple-A Sacramento.
Mayer, 23, hasn't played a major league game since late June due to left arm and right foot injuries. The Giants acquired him from the Boston Red Sox on Aug. 3 in exchange for left-hander Erik Miller, and Mayer played four games for Sacramento in mid-August before he was shut down again.
Davidson, 24, split the minor league season between Double-A Richmond and Sacramento, batting a combined .290/.361/.527 with 29 homers, 94 RBIs and 20 stolen bases in 125 games.
Both newcomers immediately joined San Francisco's starting lineup Monday night against the visiting Minnesota Twins. Davidson, playing right field and batting third, hit a first-inning single in his initial major league at-bat. Mayer served as the designated hitter and was slotted into the cleanup spot.
Left-hander Philip Abner was for assignment to clear a spot for Davidson on the 40-man roster. Abner, 24, had no decisions and a 9.64 ERA in five appearances for the Giants this year before he was optioned to Sacramento on Sunday. He pitched for the Los Angeles Angels earlier this season.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.

item.content:encoded:
Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox will take Monday off after dropping two of three games to the Tampa Bay Rays in Florida, but they return home Tuesday for a three-game series against the Cleveland Guardians with encouraging news on their closer.
Aroldis Chapman has not pitched since Sept. 13 against Kansas City. The 38-year-old left-hander has been dealing with lat tightness that kept him unavailable over the weekend.
The club indicated Chapman should be ready for the final homestand that begins Tuesday at Fenway Park.
Chapman is in the midst of another strong season. He is 3-4 with a 1.95 ERA, 34 saves and 68 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings across 52 appearances. His WHIP sits at 1.14.He has converted 34 of 36 save chances. His four-seam fastball has averaged 96.9 mph this year.
The Cuban-born reliever reached 401 career saves earlier this season. He also became the all-time strikeout leader among relief pitchers in July.
Boston clinched a wild-card berth Sunday despite a 5-1 loss to the Rays. The Red Sox are 84-72 and sit third in the AL East, 11 1/2 games behind Tampa Bay.
They have gone 52-25 since sitting 32-46 and 15 1/2 games out of first place on June 24. Interim manager Chad Tracy is 74-55 since taking over in late April.
The team holds a four-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for the second wild-card spot with six games remaining.
Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller handled recent save situations while Chapman was sidelined. Whitlock recorded his fourth save of the year last week.
Chapman is under contract for $13.3 million this season. A $13 million mutual option for 2027 becomes guaranteed if he remains healthy and passes a physical after the season. He has already surpassed the 40-inning threshold attached to that clause.
The Red Sox bullpen has been a strength throughout the year. Chapman’s availability for the Guardians series and the following set against the Chicago Cubs would give the club a clearer picture heading into the postseason.
Boston is projected to face the New York Yankees in a best-of-three Wild Card series beginning Sept. 29 on the road unless the standings shift in the final week.
The Guardians arrive at Fenway after their own late-season push. Cleveland remains in the mix for an AL Wild Card berth.
Chapman first felt the lat tightness last Tuesday. He has reported improvement through the week and was not placed on the injured list.
The Red Sox have been cautious with their veteran closer given the proximity of the playoffs. They have enough of a cushion in the wild-card race that they do not need to rush him back.
Chapman’s last outing was a scoreless ninth inning with three strikeouts against the Royals. He walked two in that appearance.
His 2026 numbers include a 12.08 strikeouts-per-nine-innings rate and just three home runs allowed.
The left-hander was named an All-Star for the ninth time this summer. He also earned All-Star honors in 2025.
Boston’s remaining regular season games are all at Fenway Park. The homestand offers a chance to get Chapman work before the postseason begins.
The clubhouse celebrated the playoff clinch Sunday night in St. Petersburg after the Houston Astros lost to Atlanta, which officially locked in Boston’s berth.
Players and staff gathered for a team photo on the field after the result became official.
The Red Sox now shift focus to finishing the regular season healthy and sharp. Chapman’s expected return is a key piece of that preparation.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. The clinch became official Sunday when the Braves beat the Astros, guaranteeing Boston a spot in the Wild Card Series starting on September 29.
The roster is not yet complete. Several key arms are still working their way back from injuries, and the next six games at Fenway Park will determine how the pitching staff looks when October arrives.
One of the biggest names on that list took a step forward this week.
Tracy Provides Update on Crochet
Garrett Crochet is closing in on a significant milestone in his comeback. Interim manager Chad Tracy said the plan is for Crochet to throw a live bullpen session against hitters early next week, with Tuesday as the hopeful target.
"Maybe early next week, a potential IBP dependent on how he feels over the next couple days," Tracy said. "Maybe early next week we'll be able to face some hitters. But yeah, tentative."
Crochet's ramp-up has been deliberate at every stage, and the Red Sox are not going to rush the left-hander into a situation he is not ready for.
Facing live hitters would represent the most significant test of Crochet's rehab to this point. He threw 30 pitches over two simulated innings earlier this month, and Tracy said at the time that everything went well. A live session against hitters is the next level up.
What Crochet Would Mean for October
Crochet's potential availability changes the shape of Boston's postseason pitching plans.
The rotation is lining up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as the likely starters for the Wild Card Series. Tolle has posted a 2.44 ERA across his last eight starts. Gray has been one of the best starters in the American League this season, carrying a 2.76 ERA.
Adding Crochet would give Tracy another weapon to deploy, albeit from the bullpen.
Tyron Guerrero returned from the injured list Sunday and looked sharp. Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, and Erik Miller round out a late-inning group that has carried the pitching staff down the stretch. Tanner Houck continues to progress through minor league rehab and remains a potential option.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Garrett Crochet is not back yet. The live bullpen is tentative. The timeline is still dependent on how his body responds day to day.
The Red Sox have been patient with this process, and that patience could pay off at exactly the right time.
Tuesday will tell the story. If Crochet gets through a live session clean, Boston's pitching picture for the postseason gets significantly deeper.

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

There were many questions the New York Yankees needed Spencer Jones to answer this season. Now, we've seen enough of him, even if it's been in a couple of disjointed stints, to get a good idea of who he is at the major league level.
The answer: pretty damn good. After struggling early, Jones has found his footing. A big reason for his ascendancy has been surprising. The Vanderbilt product has mashed left-handed pitching.
He's now logged 51 plate appearances against lefties and has slashed an eye-watering .435/.490/.761 following his homer off Minnesota Twins lefty specialist Taylor Rodgers on Sept. 15. It was the first dinger Rodgers gave up to a left-handed hitter over 133 plate appearances this season.
The sample size isn't huge, but it's relatively significant. For example, Ben Rice has 209 plate appearances against lefties out of his 622 plate appearances. For Jones, the 51 matchups against southpaws are a decent portion of his 255 total plate appearances.
One of the most impressive things about how he's performed against same-handed pitching is the amount of power he's demonstrated. Obviously, the six-foot-seven outfielder is a behemoth, but most lefties, even those who perform well against southpaws, see a drop in power in those situations. Take Rice, for instance; his slugging percentage drops from .561 against righties to .457 against left-handers. That hasn't been the case for Jones.
This has just been one part of Jones' maturation process that should have every fan feeling confident about not only his future, but his ability to contribute now.
Spencer Jones' performance against lefties has Yankees well-positioned for playoffs vs. Red Sox
Overall, Jones is hitting .259/.331/.452 with 10 homers on the season. He's been even better since being recalled on July 22, posting a .271/.337/.490 line with eight of his 10 homers coming during this most recent span.
There should be no more doubt that he should start over Trent Grisham, assuming Grisham is healthy, once the playoffs roll around. A significant part of that reasoning has to do with his performance against southpaws.
Jones has learned a lot from Cody Bellinger on how to handle those tough at-bats since he's been up in the bigs and the star left fielder has been healthy.
“When we are in the dugout, he’s one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, ‘Yo, what did you see?’ He’ll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he’s going to do next time. It’s like, all right, good to know before I go even into my first (at-bat) what this MVP is going to do for his first at-bat. It’s pretty sweet knowing that I’ve got these guys to help me out,” Jones said to The Athletic this week.
He couldn't have a better mentor. Bellinger isn't hitting lefties as much as he did last year, when he put up an insane .353/.415/.601 line, but his .287/.346/.449 performance in 2026 is plenty good, and better than what he's done against righties. In fact, Bellinger is about as balanced as they come with an .804 career OPS against left-handers and an .819 mark against righties.
We spoke about Rice earlier, but the early-season drama about his usage against lefties is a thing of the past. While he has more pop against righties, Rice's .255/.330/.457 line against southpaws is more than serviceable.
Despite having so many lefties in the lineup on a daily basis, the Yankees as a whole don't suffer much from it. The club is hitting a collective .247/.318/.422 against left-handed pitching this season, with a .740 OPS that ranks ninth. Remember, for most of that time, Aaron Judge hasn't been a factor, either.
Looking ahead, the Yankees' most likely opponent in the Wild Card series is the Red Sox, who are loaded with left-handers. In the rotation, they boast southpaws Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez, with their being a possibility that Jake Bennett makes the cut, too. In the bullpen, they'll hope to unleash Garrett Crochet, Erik Miller and old friend Aroldis Chapman.
However, rather than being overmatched, we might say that this plays into the Yankees' hands. New York can handle left-handed pitching, and those lefty bats can tee off against righties. Jones emerging as a threat against southpaws only solidifies the strength and gives the Yankees another regular who doesn't need a platoon partner, allowing them to match up only where they're vulnerable.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — When Roman Anthony returned to the Boston Red Sox three weeks ago after nearly four months on the injury list with a torn right finger ligament, it initially looked as if he had barely missed any time.
Through his first five games after he was activated Aug. 30 in New York, Anthony recorded four games with multiple hits, going 10-for-22 with two homers, two doubles and a triple. His methodical rehab, missing 101 games, paid dividends with a bat that was ready to perform.
Advertisement
But then, as so often happens in baseball, he fell out of rhythm at the plate, collecting just seven hits, including just one extra-base hit, in his next 56 plate appearances.
That’s why he found himself in an early batting practice session Friday afternoon with hitting coach John Soteropulos, tinkering in the cage with a few mechanical adjustments.
The work clicked.
Oh baby, Roman! pic.twitter.com/aP7bBEgZX0
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 18, 2026
Three pitches into the game, Anthony clubbed a solo homer for a lead, and in the second inning, he smacked a bases-loaded single to drive in two more runs as the Red Sox beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-2, snapping the Rays’ six-game win streak. The win inched the Red Sox closer to clinching a playoff berth. A Red Sox win Saturday, coupled with a Texas Rangers loss, would punch Boston’s ticket to the playoffs.
“We came out and looked really good offensively in the first part of that game, and there was a lot of energy in the dugout,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “I think guys feel it. We’re not done yet, but I definitely think they sniff it, and we’re wanting to get there for sure.”
With eight games left in the regular season, getting Anthony’s bat hot again, particularly as Willson Contreras remains day to day with a deeply bruised right hand, will be imperative for the Red Sox lineup in the postseason.
“He will,” Tracy said confidently about Anthony’s bat regaining momentum. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows. He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.”
Before Soteropulos was elevated to lead hitting coach this season after an overhaul of the coaching staff, he was the minor-league hitting coordinator and worked closely with Anthony. That relationship has helped.
Advertisement
“Me and John have been working on some things, really since I have been back,” Anthony said. “He’s amazing. He’s somebody who knows my swing so well. We have been together since I came into this org, all throughout the minor leagues. Having somebody here, somebody who knows my swing and when to talk and when to tinker. Nobody knows me better than John.
“It’s such a constant game of adjustments and looking over a span of my last few at-bats, it obviously was not where I wanted to be. I was hitting the ball on the ground, to the right side, so I was trying to get away from that. Hitting early on the field with John and with Trevor (Story) definitely helped.”
Anthony’s first-inning homer came off the bat at an estimated 107.7 mph with an estimated distance of 438 feet, marking the longest homer of his career.
But to him, the two-run single was just as important. In a rough series in Texas, the Red Sox had gone just 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position. His goal was to alleviate some pressure on the offense by simply making contact.
“That’s my job, to do everything I can to put the ball in play and find ways on base,” he said. “That’s how I have had a lot of success in the past as a leadoff hitter. So over these last games, just keep putting an emphasis on being the best leadoff hitter I can be. See as many pitches I can and try and get on base. It was a huge way to start the game. This game is all about momentum, so any time you can get something like that going, it’s huge.”
The two-run single gave the Red Sox the lead back after the Rays tied the score off Ranger Suarez in the bottom of the first. Jahmai Jones made it 4-1 in the third with his sixth homer of the year.
The insurance gave the Red Sox a cushion as Suarez was uncharacteristically spotty with command, walking a career-high five batters.
Advertisement
Still, he navigated traffic in each of the first four innings and allowed just the one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings. Reliever Wyatt Olds wiggled out of a jam in the sixth after Suarez exited, walking two batters to load the bases, then falling behind pinch hitter Jake Fraley 3-1. Olds came back to strike out Fraley.
The Red Sox faced more trouble in the ninth, with reliever Erik Miller still searching for his command. Closer Aroldis Chapman remains day to day with lat tightness, and Tracy turned to Miller for the ninth with Garrett Whitlock having a heavy load of late.
Miller allowed a run in the ninth on an infield single, a wild pitch, a walk and a groundout. He loaded the bases after a strikeout got away on a wild pitch, but escaped the jam with a groundout to close it out.
Clinching their postseason spot with a week left in the regular season would allow the Red Sox to breathe and reset some players before the postseason. But they’re not there yet. Saturday awaits.
“It just kind of felt like a playoff game,” Anthony said. “Getting into that mode is huge from an at-bat standpoint and from a big-game standpoint of constantly being the next man up.”

Roman Anthony Powers Red Sox Past Rays, Closer To Playoff Berth originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox spent much of Friday night walking a tightrope. Roman Anthony made sure they had enough of a cushion to survive. Anthony homered and drove in three runs, Ranger Suárez battled through 5 2/3 innings and the Red Sox held on for a 4-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field.
Boston improved to 84-70 with its second consecutive victory and snapped Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak. The Red Sox entered the series opener with a magic number of three to clinch an American League wild-card berth and could secure their postseason spot as early as Saturday.
It was not a comfortable victory.
Red Sox pitchers issued nine walks, including four over the final four innings. The Rays loaded the bases in both the sixth and ninth but went 0-for-13 with runners in scoring position and stranded 12 runners. Erik Miller finally ended the ninth-inning adventure by getting Chandler Simpson to ground out with the bases loaded.
Here are three takeaways from Boston's important victory.
Roman Anthony Sets Tone Immediately
Anthony did not wait long to make his presence felt. The Red Sox rookie crushed Ian Seymour's third pitch of the game 438 feet to center field, giving Boston a 1-0 lead before most of the announced crowd of 23,342 had settled into its seats.
It was Anthony's fifth home run of the season and the third leadoff homer of his young career. The Rays answered in the bottom of the first when Junior Caminero drove in Yandy Díaz with a groundout, but Anthony struck again one inning later.
Trevor Story singled and Caleb Durbin followed with another base hit. After Nate Eaton walked to load the bases, Anthony delivered a two-out single to right that scored Story and Durbin. Anthony finished 2-for-5 with three RBIs, accounting for nearly all of Boston's offense on one of the biggest nights of its season.
Jahmai Jones supplied the other run by launching a 414-foot solo homer to left in the third inning. Jones' sixth home run gave Boston a 4-1 advantage that held until the ninth.
Ranger Suárez Bends Without Breaking
Suárez rarely had a clean inning, but the left-hander consistently found his way out of trouble. The Boston starter allowed only three hits and one run while striking out five. He also issued five walks and needed 98 pitches to record 17 outs.
His best defensive moment came in the fourth inning.
Taylor Walls hit a 100-mph line drive directly back at Suárez, who made the catch before throwing to first base to double off Nick Fortes. The play erased a scoring opportunity and helped Suárez navigate another stressful inning. The left-hander improved to 8-4 and lowered his ERA to 3.27.
Wyatt Olds entered with two outs in the sixth and immediately made matters worse by issuing two walks. He recovered to strike out Jake Fraley with the bases loaded, preserving Boston's three-run advantage.
Greg Weissert provided the calmest portion of the night, allowing one hit over two scoreless innings.
Erik Miller Survives Chaotic Ninth Inning
The Red Sox carried a 4-1 lead into the ninth, but Miller turned the final three outs into a full-blown ordeal. The left-hander issued two walks and threw three wild pitches during a 32-pitch inning. Jonathan Aranda drove in one run with a fielder's choice, cutting Boston's lead to 4-2.
Tampa Bay eventually loaded the bases with two outs, bringing Simpson to the plate as the potential winning run. Miller induced a ground ball to third baseman Durbin, who completed the force play at second to end the game. Miller earned his fifth save despite allowing one run, one hit and two walks.
Boston will take the victory, especially at this stage of the season, but the nine walks gave the club another issue to clean up before October. The Red Sox will attempt to clinch their postseason berth Saturday when they continue the three-game series in Tampa Bay. The Rays are scheduled to start right-hander Freddy Peralta, while Boston has yet to announce it's starter.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Tampa Bay Rays have been the best team in the American League for much of this season, particularly at Tropicana Field.
But with one All-Star on the injured list and two others unavailable, the Red Sox came away with a 4-2 victory before a crowd of 23,342 as Roman Anthony drove in three runs.
Now the magic number to clinch a playoff spot is down to two.
Ranger Suarez (8-4) and three relievers walked nine but held the Rays to five hits. Tampa Bay was hitless in 13 at-bats with runners in scoring position and left 12 men on base.
It was an impressive victory for the Sox, considering the 93-60 Rays are close to clinching the best record in the league and home-field advantage through, at least, the American League Championship Series.
The Sox were without Ceddanne Rafaela, who isn’t expected to come off the injured list until next week. Aroldis Chapman (lat strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) were not available.
With Garrett Whitlock left in the bullpen after pitching Thursday night, the Sox used lefthander Erik Miller to get the final three outs for his first save with the team.
Miller walked two and threw three wild pitches in a wild ninth inning, giving up a run before finally getting Chandler Simpson to ground to second for the final out.
Miller had allowed five runs over 5⅓ innings and put 10 men on base in his previous six appearances.
The Sox didn’t arrive at the team hotel until close to 5 a.m. after beating the Rangers in Texas on Thursday night. The Rays had a day game at home that ended 13 hours earlier. But the Sox had more energy early on.
Anthony blasted the third pitch of the game from Ian Seymour 438 feet to center field for his fifth home run.
Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the second inning with singles. Isiah Kiner-Falefa dropped a bunt to advance the runners before Nate Eaton worked a walk to load the bases.
After Connor Wong struck out, Anthony worked the count full and lined a hard single to right field to drive in two more runs. The three RBIs matched his career high.
Jahmai Jones homered leading off the third inning, a 414-foot shot to left field.
Suarez did not handle the run support very well. He walked a hitter in each of the first four innings and threw 69 pitches. But the Rays scored only one run.
Yandy Diaz walked leading off the bottom of the first, advanced to third on a double by Jonathan Aranda, and scored on Junior Caminero’s groundout.
Suarez was done after 5⅔ innings and 98 pitches, leaving the game with a runner at second. Wyatt Olds walked Liam Hicks and Victor Mesa Jr. on 12 pitches to load the bases.
He fell behind Jake Fraley 3 and 1, then came back to strike him out swinging through a fastball at the top of the strike zone. Olds threw up his hands after finally ending the inning. It wasn’t an elegant outing, but it was ultimately an effective one.
Greg Weissert worked around a two-out double by Caminero in the seventh inning to keep the lead at three runs, then came back for a 1-2-3 eighth.

Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic.
Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs.
With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at three entering the night, will drop to either one or two depending on the outcome of Friday’s late game between the Rangers and Blue Jays.
A Rangers win would mean the Red Sox could clinch with a win on Saturday, while a Blue Jays win would necessitate a win and a Blue Jays loss.
Following a string of poor offensive performances, Friday got off to a much stronger start at the plate. Roman Anthony put the Red Sox in front with a solo home run to lead off the game, and after the Rays tied it up in the bottom half of the first, Anthony delivered again in the second with a go-ahead two-run single with the bases loaded off Rays starter Ian Seymour, an alumnus of St. John’s High School in Shrewsbury.
Anthony finished 2 for 4 with three RBI, and the Red Sox never looked back.
“Taking that first one is big,” Anthony told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “Any win you can get against a team like that it’s a great win, so it’s a great day.”
Anthony’s first-inning blast was smoked. Measured at 107.7 mph off the bat and traveling 438 feet, the solo home run to right field narrowly missed landing in Tropicana Field’s ray tank.
His two-run single in the second inning was hit even harder, coming off the bat at 108.7 mph. Anthony came through after Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the inning with singles, Isiah Kiner-Falefa moved them into scoring position with a sacrifice bunt and Nate Eaton walked to load the bases.
It was doubly encouraging given Anthony’s recent struggles at the plate. After a hot start coming off the injured list, the outfielder came into Friday batting just .137 with one extra base hit over his past 12 games.
“I’ve been grinding, but that’s the beauty of this team,” Anthony said. “You’re never down and you’re never out.”
Jahmai Jones capped off the early offense with a solo shot to lead off the top of the third.
Tampa Bay scored its early run in the first after Yandy Diaz drew a leadoff walk, advanced to third on a Jonathan Aranda double and scored on a Junior Caminero groundout. But that was all the damage the Rays could do against Ranger Suarez, who allowed one run over 5 2/3 innings while falling one out short of his third consecutive quality start.
Suarez was uncharacteristically wild, walking five batters, but he limited the damage by allowing just three hits while striking out five.
The walks almost cost the Red Sox in the sixth inning.
Still leading by three, Suarez issued his fifth and final walk to lead off the sixth before recording two quick outs to finish his outing. But Wyatt Olds came on and immediately walked the first two men he faced, loading the bases and bringing the go-ahead run to the plate.
A brief mound visit followed, and Olds dug deep and struck out pinch hitter Jake Fraley to escape the inning unscathed.
“It was a weird game all the way around, we walked nine in total, Ranger walked five but still almost completed six innings and he was very competitive with men on base,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in St. Petersburg. “He lost some counts and behind more counts today, but he was able to make really good pitches with people on base.”
Walks put the Red Sox in one more jam in the bottom of the ninth inning.
With Aroldis Chapman unavailable with a lat issue and Garrett Whitlock having pitched on Thursday, Erik Miller took the mound in the ninth and walked three men. He allowed a run to score on a Victor Mesa Jr. groundout, and the third walk to Caminero brought the winning run to the plate with two outs.
Miller struck out Ryan Vilade, but the ball got away from Connor Wong and the Rays batter reached safely to extend the game and load the bases. But Miller fought back and drew a game-ending groundout from Chandler Simpson, leaving the Rays 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position and 12 men left on base in spite of the nine walks issued by the Red Sox pitching staff.
While Miller has now walked seven batters over his last 3 1/3 innings, Tracy said he felt the left-hander looked much better on Friday despite all of the traffic.
“I thought he was way more competitive,” Tracy said. “Everything was around the zone, stuff was good, he was getting some swing and miss like he usually does so I take a lot of good out of that outing.”
The win marked Boston’s first at Tropicana Field this season, and the club hopes plenty more will follow in the days and weeks to come. The Rays have long been in the driver’s seat for the AL East title, and barring a complete collapse over the final week Tampa Bay should soon lock down the American League’s top seed and a bye to the divisional round.
That means if the Red Sox (84-70) can get past the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series, they’d be headed right back to St. Petersburg to face the Rays in a rematch of the 2021 ALDS.
But first, the Red Sox hope to pop some bottles in the Tropicana Field visitor’s clubhouse before they fly back to Boston. First pitch on Saturday is scheduled for 4:10 p.m.

Boston Red Sox fans were already going through it on Thursday night after Willson Contreras left the series finale against the Texas Rangers early after being hit by a pitch on the hand. Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse.
Whitlock is no slouch, as Red Sox fans know, and he got through the ninth frame unscathed, but fans expect to see Aroldis Chapman in moments like that. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was unavailable due to a lat issue.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said in his September 17 postgame presser that Chapman has been dealing with lat tightness for a couple of days but that he's been improving lately. Boston has classified him as day-to-day and it will routinely check on his recovery progress to gauge his availability.
The best news from Tracy on Chapman is that the team will not place him on the injured list. The Sox's bullpen has been one of their deadliest weapons all season and Chapman with his 1.95 ERA, 34 saves, blistering velocity and unmatched consistency at 38 years old has been a huge part of that success.
Aroldis Chapman injury news is a blow the Red Sox's bullpen can't afford as the playoffs near
Still, having Chapman at anything less than 100 percent is dangerous this late in the season with the playoffs on the horizon. In a tight game, one slip-up in the ninth inning could lead to disaster.
The rest of the Red Sox's bullpen is hardly in its best shape. Justin Slaten's season ended following continued flexor issues and Tyron Guerrero is still on the IL bouncing back from shoulder inflammation. Erik Miller is also dealing with a mechanical issue that has severely impacted his command over his last two outings.
If Chapman's injury is as mild as Tracy is letting on and he doesn't need an IL stint, Boston might be able to avoid disaster. But it also needs Chapman's help to clinch its playoff spot in the first place. The offense is struggling to get out to enough of a lead that it doesn't need Chapman to hold a slim margin in the late innings, but that won't fly in the postseason, especially with an injured closer.
At least the Red Sox expect some relief reinforcements in the coming days. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working towards returns from long-term injuries in a relief role and they could take some pressure off the 'pen, but neither could fill Chapman's role.
